backlog.title: What Most People Get Wrong About Evolution | Akarsh Kumar
backlog.question: What mechanisms and controls distinguish useful evolutionary accumulation from critic bias and hand-designed substrate effects?
backlog.reason: Two explicit experimental systems connect selection, novelty and learned representations; distinct from a general evolution interview.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The FER account and extrapolation to intelligence remain hypotheses.

backlog.title: Can Rewriting an AI Agent Bend the Intelligence Curve? - Zhengyao Jiang
backlog.question: What held-out evidence distinguishes harness optimisation, reward hacking and improvement of the improvement process?
backlog.reason: A concrete controlled setup can distinguish improved performance from becoming a better improver.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The publisher explicitly says better-improver status was not established.

backlog.title: The AI That Replaces Hours of Model Tuning - Frank Hutter
backlog.question: What prior and exchangeability assumptions support the posterior approximation, and where does it fail under shift or intervention?
backlog.reason: Directly addresses statistical learning structure beyond language models through a specific model family and its assumptions.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Synthetic causal priors do not automatically establish causal identification.

backlog.title: Why More Data Cannot Replace Prior Structure - Alexander Mattick
backlog.question: Which comparisons and formal assumptions support the case that prior constraints beat additional data or reward optimisation?
backlog.reason: A broad but technically specified alternative to scale-only explanations connects inference cost, statistical theory and constrained RL.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Sweeping criticism of model categories and theories needs contextual qualification.

backlog.title: How Physical AI Learns Across Language, Video and Action — Ming-Yu Liu
backlog.question: When does jointly trained video-action modelling transfer to real policies, and how is ranking fidelity measured?
backlog.reason: Concrete architecture and a relative-ranking validation criterion connect representation learning to embodied control.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Paid partnership; ranking fidelity may fail under policy distribution shift.

backlog.title: Speech Recognition Is Not a Solved Problem — Pavan Kumar Reddy
backlog.question: How do representation and streaming choices cause the reported failure modes, and what ablations support their remedies?
backlog.reason: This is a concrete study of representation, temporal inference and training signals in a nontext modality, distinct from the PolyAI interaction interview.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Paid partnership; deployed utility and architectural explanation are different claims.

backlog.title: What Building an AI Scientist Actually Requires Beyond Intelligence — Edward Hughes
backlog.question: How do held-out tasks and rubrics distinguish faithful replication and question selection from reproducing surface results?
backlog.reason: Offers both a competing theory of discovery and an operational experiment on faithful scientific replication.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Replication gains do not by themselves demonstrate creativity.

backlog.title: Strange Geometric Shapes Found Inside AIs — Tom McGrath
backlog.question: What causal interventions support manifold structure rather than an artefact of representation analysis?
backlog.reason: Specific mechanistic hypotheses and intervention methods directly target what neural networks learn and why feature decompositions may mislead.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; SAEs fracturing concepts and shared geometry are claims to test.

backlog.title: AI Is Learning at the Wrong Level of Abstraction — Matthieu Wyart
backlog.question: Under what data-generation assumptions does depth recover coarse variables and latent prediction reduce sample complexity?
backlog.reason: The random hierarchy model and sample-complexity theory directly address the mathematical anatomy of learning.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Toy hierarchical models may not transfer intact to natural data.

backlog.title: How Researchers Test AI for Hidden Goals — Apollo Research
backlog.question: How does the belief intervention isolate reward seeking from alternative behavioural explanations?
backlog.reason: A specified intervention-based method addresses latent motives and construct validity rather than merely discussing AI risk.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The o3 evidence concerns an intermediate checkpoint without safety training.

backlog.title: ARC-AGI-3 winning team - Millennia of minds, compressed into words.
backlog.question: Which components enable learning unseen game rules rather than exploiting familiar priors or scoring conventions?
backlog.reason: The benchmark change supplies a concrete counterexample distinguishing brute search, priors and adaptive abstraction.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Sponsor disclosure and leaderboard claims need careful metric interpretation.

backlog.title: The Thermodynamic AI Chip · Thomas Ahle
backlog.question: What computation and uncertainty distribution does the hardware implement, and what limits its efficiency or accuracy?
backlog.reason: Physical-noise computation and Bayesian uncertainty provide a distinct non-LLM mechanism; specification failures add a useful counterexample.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The thermodynamic segment is narrower than the title; production costs were paid by Normal Computing.

backlog.title: He won a Nobel here for AlphaFold. Then he left. - John Jumper
backlog.question: Which ablations isolate symmetry, data and architecture contributions, and what scientific questions remain outside the predictor?
backlog.reason: A strong scientific-model case study explicitly tests the value of structural priors against data and architecture.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Claims of solved folding and drug-target failure need precise scope; sponsor disclosure concerns differ across the description.

backlog.title: Intelligence is collective, not artificial — Prof. Michael I. Jordan (UC Berkeley / Inria)
backlog.question: How do inference guarantees and incentive design interact in a functioning collective intelligence system?
backlog.reason: Offers statistical methods and an explicitly different unit of analysis for intelligence beyond individual models.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Broad claims about AGI and missing error bars require precise interpretation.

backlog.title: When AI Discovers the Next Transformer — Robert Lange
backlog.question: Which parts actually co-evolve tasks, and which reported gains remain optimisation of fixed human objectives?
backlog.reason: Explicit search mechanisms and credit assignment make this distinct from generic AI-scientist forecasting.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The vision of open-ended science may exceed current demonstrated implementation.

backlog.title: What If Intelligence Didn't Evolve? It "Was There" From the Start! - Blaise Agüera y Arcas
backlog.question: What is proved or experimentally shown about ancestry depth, and which substrate conditions are necessary for the phase transition?
backlog.reason: A technical mathematical and experimental account of emergent complexity, distinct from the broader Blaise interview.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Publisher explicitly flags engineered tape boundaries, SUBLEQ counterexamples and extrapolation from replication to intelligence.

backlog.title: The Brain Is Just Specialized Agents Talking To Each Other — Dr. Jeff Beck
backlog.question: What operational tests or model-selection assumptions distinguish internal planning from equivalent lookup behaviour?
backlog.reason: Offers both a formal agency-identification problem and concrete alternative learning mechanisms.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Policy equivalence does not settle agency; olfactory origins are presented as a proposal.

backlog.title: AutoGrad Changed Everything (Not Transformers) [Dr. Jeff Beck]
backlog.question: How are object models composed, acquired and updated while preserving calibrated uncertainty and tractable inference?
backlog.reason: The warehouse-cat example and modular architecture provide a concrete alternative to monolithic language-centred learning.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Biological Bayes optimality and proposed robotic competence require supporting evidence.

backlog.title: Your Brain Doesn't Command Your Body. It Predicts It. [Max Bennett]
backlog.question: Which experiments distinguish counterfactual modelling from simpler learned behaviour, and how do they support the evolutionary sequence?
backlog.reason: Named behavioural experiments and a comparative evolutionary account offer evidence beyond LLM-only intelligence narratives.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The account synthesises several fields; language-model incapacity claims may depend on system scope.

backlog.title: The "Final Boss" of Deep Learning
backlog.question: Which categorical constructions yield implementable inductive biases and demonstrable algorithmic generalisation gains?
backlog.reason: Specific mathematical constructions connect compositional computation to architecture beyond generic geometric deep learning.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Unification language and the Hopf-fibration analogy require careful mathematical reconstruction.

backlog.title: The Mathematical Foundations of Intelligence [Professor Yi Ma]
backlog.question: What assumptions make coding-rate objectives yield transformer operations, and how are theoretical guarantees separated from empirical claims?
backlog.reason: Named mathematical mechanisms and CRATE comparisons directly match the user's foundations focus.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; YouTube removed 33:45 from the original; RSS chapters refer to the longer cut and timestamps are not interchangeable.

backlog.title: Tensor Logic "Unifies" AI Paradigms [Pedro Domingos]
backlog.question: How does predicate invention work, and under what conditions does the deductive mode preserve soundness while learning representations?
backlog.reason: A specified candidate language and learning mechanism merit inspection without accepting universal-unification claims.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; No-hallucination and unification claims may depend on restrictive assumptions.

backlog.title: He Co-Invented the Transformer. Now: Continuous Thought Machines [Llion Jones / Luke Darlow]
backlog.question: What temporal synchronisation mechanism produces adaptive computation, and which experiments isolate it from recurrent baselines?
backlog.reason: A concrete alternative architecture addresses internal computation, calibration and variable reasoning time beyond transformer scaling.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Spiral and maze analogies may overstate understanding differences.

backlog.title: Google Researcher Shows Life "Emerges From Code" [Blaise Agüera y Arcas]
backlog.question: What connects replication and merging to intelligence, and which parts are experimental results versus functionalist interpretation?
backlog.reason: Unlike the technical ALife lecture, this interview promises extended functionalist and collective-cognition arguments, so overlap is not proven duplication.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Computation-as-life claims exceed what engineered code substrates alone establish.

backlog.title: 29.4% ARC-AGI-2 🤯 (TOP SCORE!) - Jeremy Berman
backlog.question: How do natural-language candidates and verifier errors alter search efficiency and generalisation compared with executable programs?
backlog.reason: The change from Python programs to English hypotheses is a concrete experiment on representation and search, distinct from ARC solver interviews using direct grid prediction.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Expressiveness and epistemic-tree claims need operational definitions; public-leaderboard results may not generalise.

backlog.title: The Real Reason Huge AI Models Actually Work [Prof. Andrew Wilson]
backlog.question: Which priors, optimisation assumptions and complexity notions make larger models generalise better?
backlog.reason: Directly targets statistical foundations, separating model expressiveness from inductive bias with cited theoretical work.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Scaling claims may depend on compute-optimal regimes and selected model/data assumptions.

backlog.title: Type a Sentence, Get a Playable 3D World in 3 Seconds - Shlomi Fuchter & Jack Parker-Holder
backlog.question: How are persistence, action-conditioned dynamics and transfer to real agents evaluated independently of visual plausibility?
backlog.reason: Learned interactive dynamics and the sim-to-real gap promise a concrete world-model case rather than only a product demo.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Promotional language about learning reality and reliable memory may overstate limited-horizon performance.

backlog.title: Is "Thermo" AI the future? [Guillaume Verdon aka "Beff Jezos"]
backlog.question: Which distribution, mixing-time assumptions and measured energy costs support the proposed sampling advantage?
backlog.reason: A specified physical sampling mechanism and energy-efficiency argument justify reading despite the ideological second half.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Projected wafer efficiency and derivation of social inevitability from thermodynamics are separate, unverified claims.

backlog.title: AI Isn't Creative [Prof. Kenneth Stanley]
backlog.question: What controlled comparisons distinguish path-dependent evolvability from output equivalence, optimisation bias or human selection effects?
backlog.reason: The main interview offers an explicit competing account connecting representation quality, creative recombination and evolutionary history.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; FER is a hypothesis; publisher flags internal repetition and recommends the main interview from 47:58.

backlog.title: Wild breakthrough on Math after 56 years... [Exclusive]
backlog.question: How do evaluator design and search representation change discoveries, and what exactly is established by the matrix-multiplication result?
backlog.reason: Concrete algorithmic discovery and a meta-level representation shift directly address search, creativity and human-designed constraints.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Record, arithmetic-domain and generalisation claims require precise reconstruction; human problem/evaluator design remains central.

backlog.title: Build Specialist LLMs Like It’s 2019 (Randall Balestriero)
backlog.question: Under what label-relationship assumptions does the objective equivalence hold, and what transfers to representation quality or generalisation?
backlog.reason: Three concrete results connect objective structure, pretraining necessity and architectural bias, directly relevant beyond LLMs.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Narrow discriminative results do not establish that pretraining is unnecessary for generation.

backlog.title: "We need AIs with PHYSICAL experience" (Jeff Beck)
backlog.question: What assumptions create belief-reward nonidentifiability, and which interventions or priors could resolve it?
backlog.reason: The belief-reward identification problem and Bayesian-brain evidence distinguish this interview from later modular-robotics discussions.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; An identification obstruction need not imply impossibility of every form of alignment.

backlog.title: Why Program Synthesis Is Next (Kevin Ellis and Zenna Tavares)
backlog.question: How do learned libraries or in-context programs alter search complexity, and when are induction and transduction complementary?
backlog.reason: Several concrete learning systems explain how compositional models arise through search and interaction, beyond static prediction.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Program interpretability and benchmark success do not automatically establish human-like abstraction.

backlog.title: Exploring Program Synthesis: Francois Chollet, Kevin Ellis, Zenna Tavares
backlog.question: What assumptions support the gradient-descent limitation, and how might neural interpreters or active experiments change it?
backlog.reason: The multi-researcher contrast adds a distinct argument about learnability and interpreters beyond the Ellis/Tavares interview.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; A categorical inability claim may refer to specific training regimes rather than impossibility in general.

backlog.title: Test-Time Adaptation: the key to reasoning with DL
backlog.question: Which adaptation, data and voting components account for gains, and how is novelty separated from task-family reuse?
backlog.reason: A concrete adaptive perception approach provides an alternative to symbolic program synthesis on the same abstract-reasoning tasks.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Incomplete pipeline disclosure limits reproducibility and high-score interpretation.

backlog.title: Moving Beyond Surface Statistics (Apple researcher) [Iman Mirzadeh]
backlog.question: Which perturbations preserve semantics, and what alternative causes explain variance besides absence of reasoning?
backlog.reason: Concrete controlled perturbations and a competing measurement account warrant inspection even if universal limitations are overstated.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Cross-entropy training does not alone substantiate every impossibility claim in the description.

backlog.title: The Gap Between Humans and Machines Is ___ [Dr. Max Bartolo]
backlog.question: How do attribution and dynamic adversarial evaluation distinguish robust procedural learning from brittle benchmark performance?
backlog.reason: Detailed chapters and research links compensate for the visibly abbreviated prose, promising explicit investigative and evaluation methods.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; YouTube prose visibly ends mid-thought, but detailed chapters and RSS supply meaningful scope.

backlog.title: Panel discussion on ARC Prize 2024 (Zurich)
backlog.question: What evidence supports continuous concepts or explicit state over token-based search, apart from speculation about o3?
backlog.reason: Panel disagreement over representations and state adds distinct conceptual content to the separate implementation interview.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Overlaps index 79's algorithm; o3 internals are explicitly speculative rather than disclosed architecture.

backlog.title: Transformers Need Glasses! [Federico Barbero]
backlog.question: Which collapse bounds depend on length, precision and attention assumptions, and which modifications actually avoid them?
backlog.reason: A specific architectural failure mechanism with proposed modifications directly links mathematical structure to reasoning performance.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Asymptotic or finite-precision limits should not be conflated with all practical reasoning failures.

backlog.title: Can AI Improve Itself? [Chris Lu, Robert Lange, Cong Lu]
backlog.question: Why does the discovered nonconvex loss help, and does it transfer beyond the search tasks and evaluator?
backlog.reason: An explicit search-over-learning-algorithms experiment addresses how new update rules arise, distinct from later Shinka problem evolution.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Improving a training loss is narrower than recursively improving general intelligence.

backlog.title: Can Latent Program Networks Solve Abstract Reasoning? [Clement Bonnet]
backlog.question: How is the latent space trained to be searchable, and what prevents composition within a single fixed latent representation?
backlog.reason: A concrete nonstandard architecture connects continuous optimisation, program representation and limits of compositional search.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Program-manifold language need not imply recoverable symbolic programs or unrestricted composition.

backlog.title: ImageNet Moment for Reinforcement Learning? [Prof. Jakob Foerster]
backlog.question: What guarantees survive learning the drift function, and how does discovered clipping transfer across environments?
backlog.reason: A named theoretical framework and learned drift functions explain algorithm discovery beyond mere hardware throughput.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Speedups and behavioural interpretations need baseline context; publisher sources differ on Chris Lu's affiliation.

backlog.title: The ARC Prize 2024 Winning Algorithm [Daniel Franzen and Jan Disselhoff]
backlog.question: Why do probability-threshold search and multi-view scoring improve correctness, and how well calibrated are candidate probabilities?
backlog.reason: Detailed implementation and ablation questions distinguish this interview from the related panel at index 73.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; ARC task-specific structure may explain gains without establishing unrestricted abstraction.

backlog.title: LSTM: The Comeback Story? [Prof. Sepp Hochreiter]
backlog.question: How do exponential gates and matrix memory change gradient flow, capacity and computation compared with LSTM and attention?
backlog.reason: Concrete recurrent-memory architecture provides a substantive alternative to attention models beyond historical commentary.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Broad reasoning-limit claims are separate from architectural results; one reference label/link appears mismatched.

backlog.title: Neural Networks Are Elastic Origami! [Prof. Randall Balestriero]
backlog.question: How does evolution of linear regions explain delayed robustness, and which claims are exact versus empirical?
backlog.reason: Explicit mathematical representation and dynamic phenomena directly match foundational interests beyond language models.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Reference lists and chapter timestamps are uneven; geometric association alone is not a causal account.

backlog.title: The Professor Who Proved ChatGPT Can't Think — Subbarao Kambhampati
backlog.question: Which planning failures persist under distribution controls, and how do external verifiers change the reliability argument?
backlog.reason: Explicit planning counterexamples and alternative system designs qualify independently of the sensational title.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The title claims a proof of inability; description actually mixes experiments with architectural hypotheses and contains uneven reference dates.

backlog.title: How Do AI Models Actually Think? [Dr. Laura Ruis]
backlog.question: How reliable are influence-function approximations, and what evidence isolates procedural synthesis from correlated training examples?
backlog.reason: A specified attribution method provides a counterpoint to pure-retrieval accounts, with compositional and causal-agency extensions.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Attribution does not automatically establish a complete causal mechanism or human-like reasoning.

backlog.title: MIGHT THE ROBOTS TAKE OVER? [Prof. Yoshua Bengio]
backlog.question: What formal assumptions separate inference from goal-directed agency, and how do GFlowNets support compositional structure?
backlog.reason: Several explicit mathematical models promise substance despite the risk-focused title and large governance segment.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Oracle safety guarantees and compositionality claims have potentially restrictive assumptions.

backlog.title: François Chollet on OpenAI o-models and ARC
backlog.question: What makes graph-based search and reusable functions more adaptive than token generation, and how is efficiency measured?
backlog.reason: The program-graph proposal and explicit efficiency view add architectural and measurement content beyond benchmark reporting.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; o3 results were undisclosed at recording; later reference links must not be mistaken for contemporaneous discussion.

backlog.title: Don't invent faster horses - Prof. Jeff Clune
backlog.question: How is interestingness operationalised without collapsing into another fixed objective, and what demonstrates sustained open-ended growth?
backlog.reason: Multiple concrete search systems and the goal-deception problem offer a substantive account of continual creative discovery.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Publisher claims that model judges ensure authentic novelty are stronger than the described mechanism.

backlog.title: NEURAL NETWORKS ARE WEIRD! - Neel Nanda (DeepMind)
backlog.question: Which interventions establish causally necessary circuits, and how do SAE features depend on dictionary width and activation choices?
backlog.reason: An extensive technical account offers direct methods for investigating internal algorithms and distinguishing interpretation from intervention.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Readable features may omit or distort computation; publisher sources differ on the guest's age.

backlog.title: Test-Time Adaptation: A New Frontier in AI [Dr. Jonas Hübotter]
backlog.question: How does the Bayesian surrogate select data, and under which task and compute comparisons does local adaptation win?
backlog.reason: The metadata promises a specific statistical mechanism for selecting relevant learning data and comparing local with global learning.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The 30x wording may conflate model size with performance.

backlog.title: What is “reasoning” in modern AI?
backlog.question: Which part of COPRA or concept-library learning produces transferable abstraction rather than search guidance alone?
backlog.reason: Specific systems connect learned representations, search and formal verification, directly relevant to the structure of reasoning.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Formal proof success need not establish general reasoning.

backlog.title: AI Interpretability, Safety, and Meaning - Nora Belrose
backlog.question: What assumptions guarantee LEACE erasure, and how do nonlinear or higher-order cues explain residual competence?
backlog.reason: The erasure intervention and sequential learning of moments offer concrete tests of representation and learning structure.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Linear erasure may not eliminate a concept in all functional senses. RSS chapter metadata calls one implementation LISA while the description names LEACE; resolve the naming discrepancy.

backlog.title: Learning at test time in LLMs [Jonas Hübotter]
backlog.question: How is informativeness estimated and what ablations separate selection quality from additional test-time compute?
backlog.reason: This is a separate technical presentation with non-IID experiments and scaling questions, not demonstrated duplication of the interview at index 90.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Parameter-efficiency claims require matched evaluation and compute budgets.

backlog.title: Michael Levin - Why Intelligence Isn't Limited To Brains.
backlog.question: What experimental criteria distinguish learning and goal pursuit from passive dynamical responses in chemical and tissue systems?
backlog.reason: Named experimental systems and operational concepts could broaden the anatomy of intelligence beyond brains and language models.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Agency language and medical extrapolations need separation from demonstrated experiments; YouTube and RSS chapter timing differs.

backlog.title: The Hidden Math Behind All Living Systems
backlog.question: Which assumptions connect Bayesian mechanics to implementable active inference, and how is epistemic value computed for planning?
backlog.reason: The chapters expose the mathematical objects and algorithmic choices behind a substantial alternative framework of agency.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; Universal biological framing and advantages over RL are publisher claims requiring scope checks.

backlog.title: Decompiling Dreams: A New Approach to ARC?
backlog.question: How does decompiling amortized knowledge change library learning and search complexity, and what does it transfer to ARC?
backlog.reason: A named algorithm, search strategies and performance-limit chapters provide a concrete mechanism for learning reusable abstractions.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; ARC applicability may be a proposal rather than a demonstrated result.

backlog.title: The ChatGPT Paradox: Impressive Yet Incomplete
backlog.question: Which uncertainty estimands are identifiable, and how do explicit knowledge structures address novelty and inconsistent generated claims?
backlog.reason: The episode promises specific modeling structures and failure diagnoses beyond a generic critique of chatbots.
backlog.caveat: publisher framing; unverified; The chapter breadth may exceed the detail of any one proposed architecture.

backlog.title: Biologically-inspired AI and Mortal Computation

backlog.caveat: RealMedia audio/webcam only (/download/neuro01/nemenman.rm, HTTP 200) plus a slides PDF; no MP4 or transcript. Nemenman presenting, not Bialek.

backlog.title: What, (if anything) is the Objective Function of the Brain?
backlog.speaker: Tony Bell
backlog.question: Which objective does Bell end up defending (infomax, its limits, or a loop-level alternative), and does he derive any mechanism from it?
backlog.reason: The co-originator of infomax ICA questions the premise behind his own unifying principle. This is a direct attempt to say what one objective could explain about learning in the brain, at 95 minutes. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✗ · D 2 · E 1 · F 2.
backlog.caveat: No abstract; the title may signal a speculative talk rather than a derivation. MP4 verified at kitpcloud/brain04/Bell_Brain04_KITP.mp4.

backlog.title: From Bayes to Gibbs: a thermodynamic theory of learning
backlog.speaker: Sara Solla
backlog.question: Does she derive generalization error and learning curves from the Gibbs ensemble, and what does the temperature parameter mean for learning?
backlog.reason: Solla co-authored the Levin-Tishby-Solla 1990 Gibbs-ensemble theory of learning, so this talk comes from the founding Bayes-to-Gibbs programme. It should show how temperature, the partition function and generalization fall out of one ensemble. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 1 · E 2 · F 1.
backlog.caveat: Title only; may be a retrospective rather than new derivations. MP4 verified (Solla_Deeplearning23_KITP.mp4); the CC transcript is not checked.

backlog.title: Solvable models of deep learning dynamics, predictive coding and statistical learning
backlog.speaker: Andrew Saxe
backlog.question: Which closed-form dynamics (SVD mode-by-mode learning) does he derive, and how is predictive coding mapped onto the same solvable framework?
backlog.reason: The originator of exact deep-linear learning dynamics gives an 84-minute session-lead talk that carries the solvable model from stage-like learning to predictive coding and statistical learning. It is broader and longer than the "insights from the linear case" talk already in the collection. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 1 · E 2 · F 1.
backlog.caveat: No abstract; it may overlap the existing Saxe linear-case talk. MP4 verified; KITP lists a transcript.txt.

backlog.title: Inductive bias towards simplicity and feature learning in DNNs
backlog.speaker: Ard Louis
backlog.question: How does the parameter-function map produce an exponential bias towards low-complexity functions, and how does that prior interact with feature learning beyond the NNGP regime?
backlog.reason: The originator of the simplicity-bias programme, which bounds the function prior by Kolmogorov complexity, addresses why overparameterized networks generalize at all. The claim is contested and falsifiable, and it is central to module 2. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 2 · E 2 · F 2.
backlog.caveat: No abstract; a 50-minute research talk. MP4 verified; the CC transcript is not checked.

backlog.title: Theory of efficient coding and inferential computation and their relevance to auditory neural representations (Tutorial)
backlog.speaker: Bruno Olshausen
backlog.question: How does he move from redundancy reduction to sparse generative-model inference, and which representational predictions follow?
backlog.reason: The co-originator of sparse coding gives a 114-minute tutorial with slides that runs from the efficient-coding principle to inference to predicted receptive fields. That is the derive-the-mechanism structure of the bar, with the theory part transferable beyond audition. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 1 · E 2 · F 1.
backlog.caveat: Applied to hearing; it may overlap his existing Natural Scene Statistics Pt 1-2 lectures. MP4 and slides verified.

backlog.title: Information Flow on Trees, Reconstruction...and Glasses
backlog.speaker: Marc Mézard
pillars: §33 Stat Physics; §31 Prob Inference; §9 Information Theory
backlog.question: How does the reconstruction threshold on a tree map to the onset of replica symmetry breaking / clustering?
backlog.reason: The co-architect of the cavity method explains at the blackboard why tree reconstruction thresholds coincide with the dynamical glass transition, a central idea behind belief propagation and inference phase transitions. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 1 · E 2 · F 2.
backlog.caveat: Blackboard lunch talks are informal and pitched to a general KITP audience. MP4 verified (Mezard1_BBLunch_KITP.mp4).

backlog.title: Statistical Mechanics and Error Correcting Codes
backlog.speaker: Nicolas Sourlas
backlog.question: How is MAP versus bitwise-optimal decoding matched to zero versus Nishimori temperature, and how does the Shannon bound emerge?
backlog.reason: The originator of the spin-glass formulation of error-correcting codes (Sourlas 1989) explains the mapping, in which decoding is a ground-state or finite-temperature problem and the Shannon limit appears as a phase transition. It is a 72-minute blackboard talk bridging §9 and §33. Rubric: A✓ B✓ C✓ · D 1 · E 2 · F 2.
backlog.caveat: No abstract; 2004 blackboard recording, so video quality may be poor. MP4 verified (Sourlas_BlackboardLunch_KITP.mp4).

status_source.by: Gido M. van de Ven, Tinne Tuytelaars, Andreas S. Tolias
status_source.note: It shows how severe forgetting is depends on the scenario (task-, domain- or class-incremental): regularization fixes like EWC fail in class-incremental settings, while replay helps.

core.order: French 1999 first, then McCloskey & Cohen 1989 §§1-3 (via library), then van de Ven et al. 2022.

core.name: Sharp thresholds and computational gaps
core.statement: Sharp thresholds and computational gaps in random problems

For the rigorous threshold, see Ding, Sly & Sun, arXiv 1411.0650.

teaching.title: Phase transitions in computational problems, Day 1 (Simons Lectures, MIT, April 2024)

status_source.title: The Overlap Gap Property: a geometric barrier to optimizing over random structures (PNAS 2021)
status_source.note: Sharp thresholds are now theorems (Friedgut; Ding-Sly-Sun for large k). Algorithmic hardness is proved only for restricted algorithm classes (OGP, low-degree, SOS). Gaps for all polynomial algorithms remain conjectural.

core.order: Zdeborová lecture first, then Kirkpatrick & Selman (all), then Mezard-Zecchina 2002 sections 1-3, then Gamarnik for status.

core.statement: Prediction-error signatures: extinction ≠ erasure, RPE-like dopamine, blocking (parameter-sensitive; RPE reading contested by ANCCR)

The volume is on archive.org as a controlled-digital-lending loan, not open access. For the RPE strand, the free root is Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997, Science 275:1593, on Dayan's Gatsby page: https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/papers/sdm97.pdf (verified).

teaching.title: Reinforcement learning in the brain (J. Math. Psych. 53:139-154, 2009)

status_source.title: Explaining dopamine through prediction errors and beyond (Nature Neuroscience 27:1645-1655, 2024)
status_source.by: Gershman, Assad, Datta, Linderman, Sabatini, Uchida & Wilbrecht
status_source.note: Concludes that a generalized prediction error covers most findings. Ramps, sensory and motor responses, and causal accounts such as ANCCR (Jeong et al. 2022, free at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9910357/) remain contested.

core.order: Niv 2009 sections 1-4 first, then Kamin 1969, then Schultz-Dayan-Montague 1997, then Gershman et al. 2024 (with Jeong 2022 as the counter-case).

teaching.title: Building Machines That Learn and Think Like People (BBS 2017)

status_source.title: Bridging the data gap between children and large language models (Trends in Cognitive Sciences 27:990-992, 2023)
status_source.note: Quantifies the 4-5 orders-of-magnitude gap in language input. Which factors close it (innate bias, grounding, interaction, evaluation) is open.

core.order: Harlow 1949 first, then Lake et al. 2017 sections 1-4, then Frank 2023.

core.name: Innate structure and prepared learning
core.statement: Innate structure and prepared learning

Tinbergen 1951, The Study of Instinct, is on archive.org as a lending copy: https://archive.org/details/studyofinstinct0000ntin_a1t3 (verified).

teaching.title: On the generality of the laws of learning (Psychological Review 77:406-418, 1970)

status_source.title: Experimental evolution of prepared learning (PNAS 111:11750-11755, 2014)
status_source.by: Aimee S. Dunlap & David W. Stephens
status_source.note: Shows that preparedness evolves as a function of environmental reliability, which turns 'innate constraint' into a testable trade-off. Whether these are specialised modules or parameter settings of general learning is still debated.

core.order: Garcia & Koelling 1966 first, then Seligman 1970, then Dunlap & Stephens 2014. Tinbergen 1951 chs. 1-2 is optional background on innate releasing mechanisms.

core.name: Goal-directed vs habitual control
core.statement: Goal-directed vs habitual control; latent learning

root.cite: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review 55:189-208. Full text at Classics in the History of Psychology (York U.).

teaching.title: Goals and habits in the brain (Neuron 80:312-325, 2013)

status_source.title: Shifting the balance between goals and habits: five failures in experimental habit induction (JEP: General 147:1043-1065, 2018)
status_source.by: de Wit, Kindt, Knot, Verhoeven, Robbins, Gasull-Camos, Evans, Mirza & Gillan
status_source.note: Overtraining-induced habits are robust in rats but did not replicate in humans across five experiments. The model-based/model-free mapping is also contested.

core.order: Tolman 1948 first, then Dolan & Dayan 2013, then de Wit et al. 2018.

core.name: Universal law of generalization
core.statement: Universal law of generalization

teaching.by: Joshua B. Tenenbaum & Thomas L. Griffiths

status_source.title: The Universal Law of Generalization Holds for Naturalistic Stimuli (2023)
status_source.by: Raja Marjieh, Nori Jacoby, Joshua C. Peterson & Thomas L. Griffiths
status_source.note: Finds the exponential law holds across many naturalistic domains once psychological space is estimated. Its origin (Bayesian vs efficient coding, Sims 2018 doi:10.1126/science.aaq1118) remains debated.

core.order: Shepard 1987 first, then Tenenbaum & Griffiths 2001 sections 1-3, then Marjieh et al. 2023.

core.name: Weber's law and adaptation
core.statement: Weber's law, adaptation and normalization to input statistics

root.cite: Laughlin, S. B. (1981). A simple coding procedure enhances a neuron's information capacity. Z. Naturforsch. C 36:910-912. doi:10.1515/znc-1981-9-1040. Listed first-root Weber 1834 (De Pulsu, Latin) states only the constant-fraction law. Laughlin founds the claim of matching to input statistics. Free copy: the Max Planck ZfN open archive (1946-2001; Edmond dataset doi:10.17617/3.GRUJYR). The URL resolves to that archive, but a bot check blocked the PDF [unverified file].

teaching.title: Normalization as a canonical neural computation (Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 13:51-62, 2012)

status_source.title: Coding principles in adaptation (Annual Review of Vision Science 5:427-449, 2019)
status_source.by: Alison I. Weber, Kamesh Krishnamurthy & Adrienne L. Fairhall
status_source.note: Adaptation to mean and variance (Brenner et al. 2000) is robust. Whether it serves efficient coding, inference or prediction, and Weber's law's deviations at extremes, are open.

core.order: Laughlin 1981 first, then Carandini & Heeger 2012, then Weber et al. 2019 (Brenner et al. 2000 as the worked case).

core.name: Working-memory limits
core.statement: Working memory holds ~3–5 chunks; slots vs resources disputed

root.cite: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity. BBS 24:87-185. Free on the author's Missouri lab site. Listed first-root Miller 1956 (free: https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Miller/, verified) argued 7+/-2 and introduced chunking. The ~3-5 figure comes from Cowan.

teaching.title: The magical mystery four: how is working memory capacity limited, and why? (Current Directions in Psych. Sci. 19:51-57, 2010)

status_source.title: Changing concepts of working memory (Nature Neuroscience 17:347-356, 2014)
status_source.by: Wei Ji Ma, Masud Husain & Paul M. Bays
status_source.note: Argues for continuous-resource and variable-precision models over fixed slots (Zhang & Luck 2008). Slots vs resources is still disputed; the ~4 limit itself is robust but measure-dependent.

core.order: Miller 1956 (short) first, then Cowan 2010, then Cowan 2001 sections 1-3 only, then Ma, Husain & Bays 2014.

core.name: Forgetting, spacing and testing
core.statement: Retention follows environmental recurrence: forgetting, spacing, testing

root.cite: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885/1913). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (trans. Ruger & Bussenius). Full text at Classics in the History of Psychology. Ch. 7 is the forgetting curve: https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Ebbinghaus/memory7.htm (verified).

teaching.title: Reflections of the environment in memory (Psychological Science 2:396-408, 1991)
teaching.by: John R. Anderson & Lael J. Schooler

status_source.title: Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques (Psych. Sci. in the Public Interest 14:4-58, 2013)
status_source.note: Rates practice testing and distributed practice as high-utility and robust across ages, materials and delays. Optimal lag (Cepeda et al. 2006/2008) and the transfer of benefits are less settled. Murre & Dros 2015 replicated Ebbinghaus's curve: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4492928/.

core.order: Ebbinghaus chs. 1 and 7 first, then Anderson & Schooler 1991, then Dunlosky et al. 2013 (testing and spacing sections).

core.name: The positive manifold (g)
core.statement: Positive manifold (g); its cause disputed

root.cite: Spearman, C. (1904). 'General intelligence,' objectively determined and measured. American Journal of Psychology 15:201-293. Full text at Classics in the History of Psychology.

teaching.title: A dynamical model of general intelligence: the positive manifold of intelligence by mutualism (Psychological Review 113:842-861, 2006)
teaching.by: van der Maas, Dolan, Grasman, Wicherts, Huizenga & Raijmakers

status_source.title: Network models for cognitive development and intelligence (Journal of Intelligence 5:16, 2017)
status_source.by: van der Maas, Kan, Marsman & Stevenson
status_source.note: The positive manifold is among psychology's most replicated findings. Its cause (a latent g, sampling/bonds, mutualism, or process overlap) is not settled by the factor-analytic data.

core.order: van der Maas et al. 2006 sections 1-2 first, then Spearman 1904 Part I skim, then van der Maas et al. 2017.

core.name: Heuristics, biases and their successes
core.statement: Heuristics, biases and their successes

root.cite: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131. doi:10.1126/science.185.4157.1124. Cambridge UP's free publisher excerpt of the 1982 book reprints chapter 1 but stops mid-availability section: https://assets.cambridge.org/97805212/84141/excerpt/9780521284141_excerpt.pdf (verified, partial).

status_source.title: Heuristic decision making (Annual Review of Psychology 62:451-482, 2011)
status_source.note: Documents when simple heuristics match or beat complex models (ecological rationality), the 'successes' side. Which biases are robust versus artifacts of framing or format is still contested. Meehl 1954's actuarial-beats-clinical result is robust (Grove et al. 2000 meta-analysis).

core.order: Tversky & Kahneman 1974 first, then Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier 2011.

core.name: Reliability-weighted cue combination
core.statement: Reliability-weighted cue combination, near but not at optimum

status_source.title: Suboptimality in perceptual decision making (BBS 41:e223, 2018)
status_source.note: Reliability weighting is qualitatively robust, but cue combination often falls short of the optimal variance reduction. Whether 'optimality' is a useful standard is contested in the commentaries.

core.order: Ernst & Banks 2002 first, then Rahnev & Denison 2018 (cue-combination section, then the commentaries).

core.name: Typicality effects
core.statement: Typicality effects, even for well-defined categories

status_source.title: The difficulties of executing simple algorithms: why brains make mistakes computers don't
status_source.note: Extends Armstrong et al. and finds typicality effects in parity and triangle judgments even when people can state the rule. What is contested is the interpretation (graded representation vs. identification heuristics over a classical core), not the effect itself.

core.order: Rosch 1975, then Armstrong, Gleitman & Gleitman 1983 (the well-defined-category twist), then Lupyan 2013 for current status

core.name: The false-belief transition
core.statement: Explicit false-belief transition around age four

status_source.title: Foundations of theory of mind and its development in early childhood
status_source.note: The explicit transition at age four is robust. What is contested is the implicit or infant false-belief findings, which have failed to replicate across many labs, and whether the transition reflects a conceptual change or a performance change.

core.order: Wimmer & Perner 1983, then the Wellman et al. 2001 meta-analysis, then Rakoczy 2022

core.name: Receptive fields matched to natural statistics

status_source.note: Estimates how much of V1 response variance standard models explain (well under half) and lists the open problems: biased sampling, nonlinearities, context.

core.order: Olshausen lecture first, then Hubel & Wiesel 1962 (Part I and the hierarchy discussion), then Olshausen & Field 1996, then the 2005 status review

core.statement: Place, grid and attractor codes

status_source.by: Gardner, Hermansen, Pachitariu, Burak, Baas, Dunn, Moser & Moser
status_source.note: The strongest test so far of the continuous-attractor prediction (a torus that persists in sleep). What remains contested is how the attractor is wired, how it is learned, and whether place-cell maps are attractors.

core.order: Khona & Fiete review (place, grid and ring-attractor sections), then O'Keefe & Dostrovsky 1971, Hafting 2005, Kim 2017, then Gardner 2022

core.name: Consolidation and replay
core.statement: Consolidation and replay

status_source.note: Causal disruption studies support a role for ripple replay. Still contested: replay for consolidation vs. planning, and standard systems consolidation vs. multiple-trace and transformation accounts.

core.order: McClelland et al. 1995 (§§1-3), then Wilson & McNaughton 1994, then Squire & Alvarez 1995, then Joo & Frank 2018

core.statement: Neuropsychological dissociations: memory systems, blindsight, perception vs action, language vs thought, confabulation

status_source.note: Covers only the language-vs-thought strand, where the dissociation is currently most contested. No single review covers all five dissociations.

status_source.note: The effects are robust. What is contested is the inference from failure to report to failure to represent, which is the same overflow debate partial report feeds.

core.order: Sperling 1960 (Exps 1-3), then Simons & Chabris 1999 (free: http://www.chabris.com/Simons1999.pdf, verified), then Logothetis & Schall 1989 (paywalled), then Simons & Rensink 2005

core.name: Critical periods
core.statement: Critical periods, perceptual narrowing and age-of-acquisition (sharp L2 cutoff contested)

teaching.title: Critical periods in speech perception: new directions

status_source.by: Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum & Steven Pinker
status_source.note: Estimates a grammar-learning decline at around 17 years. The sharp cutoff and the model's assumptions have been disputed in later reanalyses.

core.order: Wiesel & Hubel 1963, then Werker & Hensch 2015, then Werker & Tees 1984 / Maye et al. 2002 / Mayberry 1993, then Hartshorne et al. 2018

core.statement: Degeneracy and sloppiness: many parameter sets, same function

status_source.title: Multiple models to capture the variability in biological neurons and networks
status_source.note: Experimental support for animal-to-animal conductance variability with conserved output. How general this is beyond small circuits remains open. For the sloppiness side see Transtrum et al. 2015, arXiv:1501.07668 (verified).

core.order: Sethna lecture, then Prinz et al. 2004, then Gutenkunst et al. 2007, then Edelman & Gally 2001, then Marder & Taylor 2011

core.name: Balanced, irregular spiking
core.statement: Irregular spiking with balanced excitation and inhibition

root.cite: Softky, W.R. & Koch, C. (1993). The highly irregular firing of cortical cells is inconsistent with temporal integration of random EPSPs. J Neurosci 13(1):334-350. (This poses the puzzle. The balanced-state resolution is van Vreeswijk & Sompolinsky 1996, Science 274:1724, doi:10.1126/science.274.5293.1724, paywalled)

status_source.title: What is the dynamical regime of cerebral cortex?
status_source.note: Argues that cortex is loosely balanced and inhibition-stabilized rather than in the tight balanced state of van Vreeswijk & Sompolinsky. What remains contested is the degree of balance.

core.order: Softky & Koch 1993, then Shadlen & Newsome 1998, then van Vreeswijk & Sompolinsky 1996, then Ahmadian & Miller 2021

core.name: Low-dimensional structure
core.statement: Low-dimensional structure in natural data and neural population activity

root.cite: Tenenbaum, J.B., de Silva, V. & Langford, J.C. (2000). A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Science 290:2319-2323. doi:10.1126/science.290.5500.2319

teaching.title: Dimensionality reduction for large-scale neural recordings

status_source.title: Interpreting neural computations by examining intrinsic and embedding dimensionality of neural activity
status_source.note: Separates intrinsic from embedding dimensionality. Low dimensionality is task-dependent and contested by high-dimensional power-law findings (Stringer et al. 2019).

core.order: Tenenbaum 2000, then Pope 2021, then Cunningham & Yu 2014, then Churchland 2012 and Gallego 2017, then Jazayeri & Ostojic 2021

core.name: Processing near physical limits
core.statement: Processing near physical limits: photon and molecule counting, energy per bit, energy paid for accuracy

root.cite: Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne 1942, Energy, quanta, and vision, J Gen Physiol 25:819-840, doi:10.1085/jgp.25.6.819

teaching.title: Thinking about the brain (Les Houches lectures, 2001)
teaching.length: long lecture notes, roughly 100 pages [page count unverified]

status_source.title: Direct detection of a single photon by humans
status_source.note: The rod's single-photon response is robust. Whether a person can consciously report a single photon is contested: this study finds a small above-chance effect and has not been widely replicated. It does not address the energy-per-bit strand.

core.order: Bialek lectures (photon counting, then the Berg-Purcell limit) first, then HSP 1942 in full, then Tinsley 2016

core.name: Heavy-tailed, scale-invariant natural data
core.statement: Natural data are heavy-tailed and scale-invariant, incl. Zipf and the law of abbreviation

root.cite: Field 1987, Relations between the statistics of natural images and the response properties of cortical cells, JOSA A 4:2379-2394, doi:10.1364/JOSAA.4.002379

teaching.title: Natural Image Statistics and Neural Representation (Annu Rev Neurosci 2001)

status_source.title: Zipf's word frequency law in natural language: A critical review and future directions
status_source.note: Near-Zipfian word frequencies are robust across languages. The review argues that many proposed explanations are untestable or explain too little. Image 1/f scaling is robust on average, though it varies with scene type.

core.order: Simoncelli & Olshausen review first, then Field 1987, then Piantadosi 2014

core.name: Productive, systematic generalization
core.statement: Productive, systematic generalization and structure dependence

root.cite: Berko 1958, The child's learning of English morphology, Word 14:150-177, doi:10.1080/00437956.1958.11659661

status_source.title: Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network
status_source.note: In its instruction-learning experiments, people generalize systematically but not perfectly and show predictable error biases. The paper argues that neural networks can match this after meta-learning, which reopens Fodor & Pylyshyn's argument.

core.order: Berko 1958 first, then Fodor & Pylyshyn 1988 section 3, then Lake & Baroni 2023

core.name: Learners regularize and create structure
core.statement: Learners regularize input and create structure

root.cite: Senghas, Kita & Ozyurek 2004, Children creating core properties of language: evidence from an emerging sign language in Nicaragua, Science 305:1779-1782, doi:10.1126/science.1100199

status_source.title: The cognitive roots of regularization in language
status_source.note: Regularization replicates in the lab. The authors separate a domain-general, load-driven source from a language-specific one. How strong it is depends on age, load and task.

core.order: Senghas 2004 first, then Hudson Kam & Newport 2005, then Ferdinand et al. 2019

core.name: Predictability drives comprehension
core.statement: Predictability drives comprehension cost (log form contested; garden paths)

root.cite: Kutas, M. & Hillyard, S. A. (1984). Brain potentials during reading reflect word expectancy and semantic association. Nature 307:161-163. doi:10.1038/307161a0

teaching.title: Thirty years and counting: Finding meaning in the N400 component of the ERP (Annu Rev Psychol 2011)

status_source.title: Large-scale evidence for logarithmic effects of word predictability on reading time
status_source.by: Shain, Meister, Pimentel, Cotterell & Levy 2024, PNAS 121:e2307876121
status_source.note: That predictability affects processing cost is robust. Whether the relation is logarithmic is contested: this reanalysis of six datasets supports a log effect, against the linear result of Brothers & Kuperberg 2021. Garden-path costs are larger than surprisal predicts.

core.order: Kutas & Federmeier 2011 first, then Kutas & Hillyard 1980 and 1984, then Smith & Levy 2013, then Shain et al. 2024 alongside Brothers & Kuperberg 2021

core.name: Convergence and contingency
core.statement: Convergent evolution, including of cognition, alongside contingency

root.cite: Emery & Clayton 2004, The mentality of crows: convergent evolution of intelligence in corvids and apes, Science 306:1903-1907, doi:10.1126/science.1098410

status_source.title: Contingency and determinism in evolution: Replaying life's tape (Science 362:eaam5979, 2018)
status_source.note: Lab and natural replay experiments show both convergence and contingency. Which one dominates depends on scale and on how similar the starting points are. Note that this review covers evolution in general, not cognition specifically.

core.order: Emery & Clayton 2004 first, then Blount et al. 2008, then Blount, Lenski & Losos 2018

core.name: Cumulative culture
core.statement: Cumulative culture

root.cite: Tomasello, Kruger & Ratner 1993, Cultural learning, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 16:495-552, doi:10.1017/S0140525X0003123X

teaching.title: Language Learning, Language Use, and The Evolution of Linguistic Structure (SFI)

status_source.title: What is cumulative cultural evolution? (Proc R Soc B 285:20180712, 2018)
status_source.note: Cumulative culture is robust in humans and in lab transmission chains. Whether non-human animals have it is contested, and so are its defining criteria. Open-ended cumulative culture has been shown only in humans.

core.order: Tomasello 1993 target article (skip commentaries) first, then Tennie et al. 2009, then the Kenny Smith lecture with Kirby et al. 2008, then Mesoudi & Thornton 2018
